title: Linked List, Trees, Graphs
summary: Reverse, cycle, BFS and DFS, shortest path, topological sort, union-find

guide.title: Data that points to other data
points: Linked lists, trees and graphs model relationships: next song, parent folder, friend of a friend, road between cities.
Product companies (Amazon, Microsoft, Flipkart) ask tree and graph questions in almost every interview loop.
Two traversals, depth-first (DFS) and breadth-first (BFS), solve most of them.

guide.title: Where you meet these structures
points: Linked lists: browser history, music playlists, LRU caches, undo chains.
Trees: folders on disk, the HTML DOM, company org charts, database indexes (B-trees), autocomplete (tries).
Graphs: Google Maps roads, LinkedIn connections ("2nd degree" is BFS), course prerequisites (topological order), network routing.
Build tools (npm, Maven, Gradle) order dependencies with a topological sort and reject cycles.

guide.title: Nodes and edges
points: Linked list: each node has a value and a pointer to the next node. No index; walk from the head.
Binary tree: each node has up to two children. Height decides the cost; a balanced tree has height log n.
Graph: nodes plus edges, stored as an adjacency list (for each node, its neighbours).
In these problems the input is given as text (level order for trees, edge pairs for graphs) and the starter builds the structure for you.

guide.title: Build an adjacency list
points: The most common graph setup: n nodes numbered 0 .. n − 1 and a list of edges [u, v].

code.python:
adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
for u, v in edges:
    adj[u].append(v)
    adj[v].append(u)     # drop for a directed graph

guide.title: BFS: shortest path in steps
points: Start from the source, visit all neighbours, then their neighbours: level by level with a queue.
The first time BFS reaches a node is by the fewest edges. Mark nodes visited when you add them to the queue.
Level-order traversal of a tree is the same idea.

guide.title: DFS on trees: answer from the children
points: Most tree questions are "ask the left subtree, ask the right subtree, combine": height, diameter, path sums, balanced check.
Linked lists: slow and fast pointers find the middle and detect cycles; reversing needs three pointers (prev, cur, next).

guide.title: Visit everything once
points: BFS and DFS cost O(V + E): every node and edge is handled once.
Tree operations cost O(height): log n when balanced, n when the tree is a chain.
Weighted shortest path needs Dijkstra (a priority queue): O(E log V).

guide.title: What breaks pointer and graph code
points: Forgetting the visited mark: cycles make DFS or BFS run forever.
Null children: check node before reading node.left; an empty tree is a valid input.
Losing the rest of a linked list by changing next before saving it.
Deep DFS recursion on a long chain can overflow the stack; use an explicit stack or BFS.

guide.title: For advanced learners and interviews
points: Topological sort (Kahn: repeatedly remove nodes with no incoming edges) orders tasks and detects cycles.
Union-Find (disjoint set) answers "are these connected?" almost in O(1); used in Kruskal minimum spanning tree.
Binary search trees keep values sorted: in-order traversal gives sorted output; validate with min / max bounds.
Next: mix these with DP (DP on trees, shortest paths) and you are ready for most interview rounds.

problems.title: Reverse a linked list
problems.statement: The list is given as its values from head to tail. Build or walk it and return the values reversed.
inputFormat: values: integers separated by spaces (may be empty)
problems.hint: Keep prev, cur and next while relinking.

problems.title: Detect a cycle
problems.statement: next[i] is the node after node i, or -1. Starting at head, return true if you ever come back to a visited node.
inputFormat: next: integers separated by spaces (may be empty)
problems.hint: Slow moves one step, fast moves two.

problems.title: Maximum depth of a tree
problems.statement: The tree is given in level order. Return the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down.
inputFormat: tree: a binary tree in level order, "null" for a missing child
problems.hint: Process level by level, or recurse: 1 + max(left, right).

problems.title: Level order traversal
problems.statement: The tree is given in level order with "null" markers. Return the values grouped by level, one level per line (return an array of arrays).
inputFormat: tree: a binary tree in level order, "null" for a missing child
problems.hint: BFS: handle one whole level at a time.

problems.title: Count connected groups
problems.statement: An undirected graph has nodes 0..n-1. Each edge line is "u v". Return the number of connected groups.
inputFormat: edges: a count k, then k lines of integers
problems.hint: Union-find, or DFS from every unvisited node.

problems.title: Shortest path (unweighted)
problems.statement: In an undirected graph with nodes 0..n-1, return the fewest edges from start to end, or -1.
inputFormat: edges: a count k, then k lines of integers
problems.hint: BFS from start; the first visit is the shortest.

problems.title: Course schedule order
problems.statement: Courses are 0..n-1. A line "a b" means course a must be done before b. Return one order that finishes all, always taking the smallest available course; return [-1] if there is a cycle.
inputFormat: prerequisites: a count k, then k lines of integers
problems.hint: Kahn's algorithm with the smallest available node first.

problems.title: Redundant connection
problems.statement: A tree with nodes 1..n got one extra edge. The edges are listed one per line. Return the last listed edge that closes a cycle.
inputFormat: edges: a count k, then k lines of integers
problems.hint: Union-find: the edge whose ends are already joined.
